question.text: In the opposite figure: m(arc AB) = 100°.
question.stem: Do the inscribed angles ∠AEB, ∠ADB et ∠ACB include the same arc?
question.notes: Bullets are diamond-marked, not numbered; labelled 1-3 by me. Heading is 'Think and Discuss'.

answers.answer: Yes
solution: ∠AEB, ∠ADB and ∠ACB all have their sides passing through A and B.
They are inscribed angles and they all face the arc AB.
So they include the same arc AB.

checks.resolve_answer: Yes. ∠AEB, ∠ADB and ∠ACB are all inscribed angles that include (subtend) the same arc AB.

question.text: In the opposite figure: m(arc AB) = 100°.
question.stem: Find m(∠AEB), m(∠ADB), m(∠ACB). What do you notice?
question.notes: Bullets are diamond-marked, not numbered; labelled 1-3 by me. Heading is 'Think and Discuss'.

answers.answer: m(∠AEB) = 50°, m(∠ADB) = 50°, m(∠ACB) = 50°. They are all equal.
solution: An inscribed angle is half the arc it includes.
We notice that the three angles are equal, 50° each.

checks.resolve_answer: m(∠AEB) = 50°, m(∠ADB) = 50°, m(∠ACB) = 50°. They are all equal, because each is half of m(arc AB) = 100°.

question.text: In the opposite figure: m(arc AB) = 100°.
question.stem: Do the inscribed angles that include equal arcs in measure are equal in measue? Explain your answer.
question.notes: Bullets are diamond-marked, not numbered; labelled 1-3 by me. Heading is 'Think and Discuss'.

answers.answer: Yes, inscribed angles that include arcs of equal measure (in the same circle or congruent circles) are equal in measure.
solution: Each inscribed angle equals half the measure of the arc it includes.
If the two arcs have equal measures, their halves are equal.
So the two inscribed angles are equal in measure.

checks.resolve_answer: Yes. Each inscribed angle is half the measure of the arc it subtends. In the same circle or in congruent circles, equal arcs give equal halves, so the angles are equal.
checks.agreed_on: the gradable answer (Yes); the explanation is not checked

question.text: In the opposite figure: M and N are two intersecting circles at A and B. line AC intersects the circle M at C and intersects the circle N at D, line AE intersects the circle M at E, and the circle N at F. Prove that: $m(\angle EBC) = m(\angle FBD)$

answers.answer: m(∠EBC) = m(∠FBD), proved by using equal inscribed angles at A and vertical angles.
solution: In circle M, ∠EBC and ∠EAC are inscribed angles including the same arc EC.
So m(∠EBC) = m(∠EAC) (1).
In circle N, ∠FBD and ∠FAD are inscribed angles including the same arc FD.
So m(∠FBD) = m(∠FAD) (2).
∠EAC and ∠FAD are vertical angles, so m(∠EAC) = m(∠FAD) (3).
From (1), (2) and (3): m(∠EBC) = m(∠FBD) (Q.E.D.).

checks.resolve_answer: In circle M, ∠EBC and ∠EAC are inscribed angles subtending the same arc EC, so m(∠EBC) = m(∠EAC). ∠EAC and ∠FAD are vertical angles, so m(∠EAC) = m(∠FAD). In circle N, ∠FAD and ∠FBD are inscribed angles subtending the same arc FD, so m(∠FAD) = m(∠FBD). Hence m(∠EBC) = m(∠FBD).

question.text: Are each two chords not intersecting inside a circle and subtended by two congruent arcs are parallel? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: No. Two chords that do not meet inside the circle and cut off equal arcs need not be parallel, because they can meet outside the circle.
solution: Equal arcs give equal chords, as in example-3: AD = BE because the arcs are equal.
Chords that do not cross inside the circle either do not meet at all (parallel) or meet outside the circle.
In example-3, the equal chords AD and BE meet at the point C outside the circle.
So these chords are not parallel, and equal arcs alone do not make the chords parallel.
Answer: No, not always.

checks.resolve_answer: No. Chords subtended by congruent arcs are equal in length, but equal chords that do not meet inside the circle need not be parallel (e.g. the equal non-parallel legs of an isosceles trapezoid inscribed in a circle). Only chords that cut off (intercept between them) equal arcs are parallel.
checks.agreed_on: the gradable answer (No); the explanation is not checked

question.text: In the opposite figure: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two equal chords in length in the circle, $\overline{AB}\cap\overline{CD}=\{E\}$. Prove that: the triangle ACE is an isosceles triangle.

answers.answer: △ACE is isosceles because m(∠ACE) = m(∠CAE), so EA = EC.
solution: AB = CD, so m(arc AB) = m(arc CD).
Arc AB = arc AC + arc CB and arc CD = arc CA + arc AD.
Subtract arc AC from both sides: m(arc CB) = m(arc AD).
∠CAB includes arc CB and ∠ACD includes arc AD.
So m(∠CAE) = m(∠ACE).
In △ACE, equal angles mean EA = EC, so the triangle is isosceles (Q.E.D.).

checks.resolve_answer: AB = CD, so m(arc AB) = m(arc CD). Subtracting the common arc between them gives m(arc AD) = m(arc CB). Therefore the inscribed angles subtending these arcs are equal: m(∠ACD) = m(∠CAB), that is m(∠ACE) = m(∠CAE). So in triangle ACE, EA = EC and the triangle is isosceles.

question.text: In the opposite figure: $AB=AC$, $E\in\widehat{BC}$. Prove that: $m(\angle AEB)=m(\angle AEC)$.

answers.answer: m(∠AEB) = m(∠AEC), because they include equal arcs AB and AC.
solution: AB = AC, so m(arc AB) = m(arc AC).
∠AEB is inscribed and includes arc AB.
∠AEC is inscribed and includes arc AC.
Inscribed angles on equal arcs are equal.
So m(∠AEB) = m(∠AEC) (Q.E.D.).

checks.resolve_answer: AB = AC, so m(arc AB) = m(arc AC) (equal chords give equal arcs). ∠AEB and ∠AEC are inscribed angles subtending these equal arcs, so m(∠AEB) = m(∠AEC).

question.text: What is the number of bisectors of $\angle BEC$? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: An angle has exactly one bisector, so ∠BEC has one bisector.
solution: A bisector of an angle is the ray from its vertex that divides the angle into two equal angles.
Only one such ray exists, because it must make each part half of m(∠BEC).
So ∠BEC has exactly one bisector.
Answer: 1.

checks.resolve_answer: 1. An angle has exactly one bisector, because there is only one ray inside the angle that divides it into two equal angles.

Equal angles on one base and one side are not found, so no circle passes through A, B, C, D.

question.text: Which of the following figures can have a circle passing through the points A, B, C and D? Mention the reason.

answers.answer: Yes: ∠DAC and ∠DBC are equal and on the same base DC and the same side.
solution: EA = ED, so m(∠EDA) = m(∠EAD).
EB = EC, so m(∠EBC) = m(∠ECB).
AD ∥ BC, so m(∠DAC) = m(∠ACB) and m(∠ADB) = m(∠DBC).
So m(∠DAC) = m(∠ACB) = m(∠EBC) = m(∠DBC).
So m(∠DAC) = m(∠DBC), both drawn on base DC and on one side of it.
So A, B, C, D lie on one circle.

question.text: Which of the following figures can have a circle passing through the points A, B, C and D? Mention the reason.

answers.answer: Yes: ∠ADB and ∠ACB are equal and on the same base AB and the same side.
solution: In the rectangle, AD = BC, AB is common and m(∠DAB) = m(∠CBA) = 90°.
So △DAB and △CBA are congruent, so m(∠ADB) = m(∠ACB).
Both are drawn on base AB and on one side of it.
So A, B, C, D lie on one circle.

checks.resolve_answer: Yes. A rectangle has opposite angles that are right angles, so they are supplementary (90° + 90° = 180°). Equivalently, ∠ADB = ∠ACB. So a circle passes through A, B, C and D.

question.text: Which of the following figures can have a circle passing through the points A, B, C and D? Mention the reason.
